### 🎯 Practical Learning Objectives (Week 11)

This week is a **revision and integration** of what you have learned so far. By the end of this practical session, you should be able to:

- **Formulate** a simple **data science question** from a real or sample dataset.
- **Carry out** basic **EDA** (loading, cleaning, summarising, visualising).
- **Apply** at least **one analysis or model** you have seen before (correlation, regression, clustering, association rules, hypothesis test, simple prediction).
- **Interpret** results in **plain language** and connect them to a real-world context.
- **Document** your work clearly in a **notebook-style report**.

> 💡 Think of this as a **mini-project** that brings together ideas from Weeks 1–10. In the course outline: *"Mini-project – predictive modelling, data mining, and BI dashboard development."*

> 📌 **How this notebook works.** The notebook is already filled in with a **worked example** on the `heart.csv` data so that every chunk runs. You will **replace the dataset, variables and interpretation with your own**. The worked example shows the *method*, not the answer to your project.

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
**Dataset description (worked example).** `heart.csv` is an anonymised public teaching dataset of 303 patients tested for heart disease (a version of the UCI Cleveland data). One row = one patient. Key variables: `age` (years); `sex` (1 = male, 0 = female); `trestbps` (resting blood pressure, mm Hg); `chol` (serum cholesterol, mg/dl); `thalach` (maximum heart rate achieved during a stress test, beats per minute); `target` (a 0/1 diagnosis indicator).

**Main question.** *Is the maximum heart rate achieved related to age, and does it differ between the two `target` groups?*

> ⚠️ **Ethics note.** This is a teaching dataset; its results must **not** be used for clinical decisions. Also be aware that public copies of this file disagree about whether `target = 1` means "disease" or "no disease", so we use the neutral labels `target = 0` and `target = 1` and make no clinical claim.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

## 2. Loading Required Packages

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Helper: regression metrics used in Week 5
metrics <- function(y, yhat) {
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((y - yhat)^2)),
    MAE  = mean(abs(y - yhat)),
    R2   = 1 - sum((y - yhat)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2))
}
```

## 4. Light Data Cleaning

Before analysis we may need to handle **missing values**, remove **duplicates**, and convert **data types**. Use only what your dataset needs: do not over-clean.

```{r missing}
colSums(is.na(df))                 # missing values per column
```

```{r duplicates}
duplicates_count <- sum(duplicated(df))
cat("Number of duplicate rows:", duplicates_count, "\n")

df <- distinct(df)                 # keep one copy of each row
cat("New shape after removing duplicates:", dim(df), "\n")
```

*Worked example.* (1) There were **no missing values**, so no imputation was needed (imputing when nothing is missing would only add noise). (2) One **exact duplicate row** was found and removed, because a repeated patient record would be counted twice and slightly distort means and tests. The binary `target` was converted to a factor only for plotting.

## 5. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Now explore the data in relation to your **main question**. Suggested steps:

- Look at **distributions** (histograms, boxplots) of key numerical variables.
- Look at **counts** (bar charts) for important categorical variables.
- Examine **relationships** (scatter plots, group means, correlations).

### 5.1 Distributions of Numerical Variables

```{r hist}
num_col <- "thalach"          # TODO: change to a numeric variable related to your question

ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[num_col]])) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = paste("Distribution of", num_col), x = num_col, y = "Density")
```

### 5.2 Frequency of a Categorical Variable

```{r bar}
cat_col <- "target"           # TODO: change to a categorical variable

ggplot(df, aes(x = factor(.data[[cat_col]]))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(title = paste("Counts of", cat_col), x = cat_col, y = "Count")
```

### 5.3 Relationship Between Two Numerical Variables

```{r scatter}
x_col <- "age"                # TODO: change
y_col <- "thalach"            # TODO: change

pair_df <- df |> select(all_of(c(x_col, y_col))) |> drop_na()

ggplot(pair_df, aes(x = .data[[x_col]], y = .data[[y_col]])) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = paste(y_col, "versus", x_col), x = x_col, y = y_col)

ct <- cor.test(pair_df[[x_col]], pair_df[[y_col]])
cat(sprintf("Correlation between %s and %s: r = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f], p = %s\n",
            x_col, y_col, ct$estimate, ct$conf.int[1], ct$conf.int[2], format.pval(ct$p.value, digits = 3)))
```

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
*Worked example.*

- `thalach` is roughly bell-shaped with a slight left tail (mean about 149.6 bpm).
- The two `target` groups are of similar size (138 vs 164 patients), so no serious class imbalance.
- `age` and `thalach` have a **moderate negative correlation** (r = −0.395, 95% CI [−0.486, −0.296]): older patients reach a lower maximum heart rate.
- The scatter plot supports a roughly linear decline of about 0.9 bpm per year of age, with wide scatter around the line.

## 6. Main Analysis or Model (Choose One Approach)

Choose **one** of the following options (depending on your dataset and question):

1. **Simple Linear Regression** – predict a numerical target from one numerical predictor (Week 5).
2. **Group Comparison** – compare means between two groups (t-test) or test an association (chi-square) (Week 7).
3. **Clustering** – group similar records with k-means (Week 6).
4. **Association Rules (Market Basket)** – if your data are transactional with items per basket (Week 6; use `grocery_transactions.csv`).

Your lecturer may specify which option to use. Below are **templates for options 1–3**; adapt as needed.

### 6.1 Option A: Simple Linear Regression (Prediction)

```{r regression}
# >>> SOLUTION
feature_col <- "age"        # predictor
target_col  <- "thalach"    # target

model_data <- df |> select(all_of(c(feature_col, target_col))) |> drop_na()
f <- as.formula(paste(target_col, "~", feature_col))

# 80/20 split
set.seed(42)
idx   <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.8 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[idx, ]; test <- model_data[-idx, ]

model <- lm(f, data = train)
cat(sprintf("Model: %s = %.3f + %.3f x %s\n", target_col, coef(model)[1], coef(model)[2], feature_col))
confint(model)

round(metrics(test[[target_col]], predict(model, test)), 3)

# Variability of the metrics over 200 random splits
set.seed(42)
reps <- t(replicate(200, {
  i <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.8 * nrow(model_data)))
  m <- lm(f, data = model_data[i, ])
  metrics(model_data[[target_col]][-i], predict(m, model_data[-i, ]))
}))
tibble(metric = colnames(reps), mean = colMeans(reps), sd = apply(reps, 2, sd)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
# <<< SOLUTION
```

```{r regression-plot}
# >>> SOLUTION
ggplot(model_data, aes(.data[[feature_col]], .data[[target_col]])) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = paste(target_col, "versus", feature_col, "with regression line"),
       x = feature_col, y = target_col)
# <<< SOLUTION
```

### 6.2 Option B: Group Comparison (Means / t-Test)

```{r group-comparison}
# >>> SOLUTION
group_col   <- "target"
numeric_col <- "thalach"

df |>
  group_by(.data[[group_col]]) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(.data[[numeric_col]]), sd = sd(.data[[numeric_col]]), .groups = "drop")

tt <- t.test(as.formula(paste(numeric_col, "~", group_col)), data = df)       # Welch
tt

g  <- split(df[[numeric_col]], df[[group_col]])
sp <- sqrt(((length(g[[1]]) - 1) * var(g[[1]]) + (length(g[[2]]) - 1) * var(g[[2]])) /
           (length(g[[1]]) + length(g[[2]]) - 2))
cat(sprintf("Cohen's d = %.2f\n", (mean(g[[2]]) - mean(g[[1]])) / sp))

ggplot(df, aes(factor(.data[[group_col]]), .data[[numeric_col]], fill = factor(.data[[group_col]]))) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste(numeric_col, "by", group_col), x = group_col, y = numeric_col)

# Is the group difference just an age effect? Adjust for age (multiple regression)
summary(lm(thalach ~ age + target, data = df))$coefficients
# <<< SOLUTION
```

### 6.3 Option C: Clustering (k-Means)

```{r clustering}
# >>> SOLUTION
cluster_vars <- c("age", "trestbps", "chol", "thalach", "oldpeak")
x <- df |> select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |> drop_na() |> scale()      # standardise: mean 0, sd 1

set.seed(42)
sil <- map_dfr(2:6, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(x, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  tibble(k = k, avg_silhouette = mean(cluster::silhouette(km$cluster, dist(x))[, "sil_width"]))
})
sil

km <- kmeans(x, centers = 2, nstart = 25)
df |> select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |> drop_na() |>
  mutate(Cluster = factor(km$cluster)) |>
  group_by(Cluster) |>
  summarise(n = n(), across(everything(), ~ round(mean(.x), 1)))
# <<< SOLUTION
```

> ✏️ **Student Task 6 – Main Analysis Interpretation:**
> In 4–6 sentences, interpret the key result from your chosen method.
> - **Regression:** what does the slope mean? Is the model fit good?
> - **Group comparison:** which group has the higher mean? Is the difference statistically significant, and how large is it?
> - **Clustering or association rules:** briefly describe two interesting patterns.

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
*Worked example (regression and group comparison).* The regression slope is about −0.94 bpm per year on the training split (95% CI −1.25 to −0.64): each additional year of age is associated with a maximum heart rate roughly 1 bpm lower. On the held-out 20% the model has RMSE = 19.8 bpm and R² = 0.23, but over 200 random splits the mean is RMSE = 21.2 (SD 1.8) and R² = 0.12 (SD 0.10), so the single split was optimistic: age explains roughly an eighth of the variation, which is useful for trend and poor for individual prediction. The `target = 1` group has a **higher** mean `thalach` (158.4 vs 139.1 bpm; Welch t = −7.90, p < 0.001; difference 19.3 bpm, 95% CI 14.5 to 24.1; Cohen's d = 0.93, a large effect). The `target = 0` group is also older on average (56.6 vs 52.6 years), so part of the gap could be an age effect; the age-adjusted model still shows a clear difference of about 16 bpm (t = 6.9). Clustering found only weak structure (average silhouette 0.24 at k = 2, falling to 0.20 by k = 6), so we would not interpret the clusters as real patient subtypes.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->

> 🧪 **Student Activity – Mini-Report Outline:**

1. **Title and Dataset** – e.g. "Analysis of Maximum Heart Rate in a Cardiac Teaching Dataset".
2. **Main Question** – clearly state the question you tried to answer.
3. **Data & Methods** – 4–6 sentences summarising the data you used and the methods (EDA, regression, tests, ...).
4. **Key Findings** – 3–5 bullet points with the most important results (with effect sizes and confidence intervals).

6. **Next Steps** – 2–3 ideas for further analysis or for turning this into a bigger project.

<!-- >>> SOLUTION -->
### Example mini-report (worked example)

**1. Title and dataset.** Maximum heart rate, age and diagnosis group in 302 patients (anonymised public teaching dataset, `heart.csv`).

**2. Main question.** Is the maximum heart rate achieved during a stress test related to age, and does it differ between the two `target` groups?

**3. Data and methods.** After removing one duplicate row (302 patients, no missing values) we explored distributions and relationships graphically. We fitted a simple linear regression of `thalach` on `age` (80/20 split, seed 42, 200 repeated splits to measure variability), compared the two groups with a Welch t-test and Cohen's d, and checked the group difference with an age-adjusted regression. A k-means analysis on five standardised clinical variables was used to look for subgroups.

**4. Key findings.**

- Maximum heart rate falls by about 0.9 bpm per year of age (r = −0.395).
- Age explains only about 12% of the variance in held-out data (mean R² = 0.12, SD 0.10 over 200 splits; RMSE about 21 bpm).
- The `target = 1` group reaches a higher maximum heart rate (about 19 bpm, d = 0.93), and the difference persists after adjusting for age.
- Clustering shows weak structure (average silhouette 0.24 at best).

**5. Limitations.** Observational data, so no causal claims; unclear coding of `target` in public copies of the file; only 302 patients; no information on medication or fitness, which affect heart rate.

**6. Next steps.** Fit a multiple regression with sex, blood pressure and cholesterol; try a logistic regression to predict `target`; validate with an independent dataset.
<!-- <<< SOLUTION -->
